A thread-pool stress probe stayed consistent. The 21 tests are meaningful, and three of them are real concurrency tests that synchronize threads with a barrier. strengths: All spec requirements met: available = on_hand - held, UnknownProduct for non-catalog SKUs (including unhashable values), 0 for catalog SKUs missing from the dict, OutOfStock and ValueError raised correctly, and settle-at-most-once enforced for every commit/release combination

Correct locking: the check-then-act in reserve and the settle in commit/release are atomic under one lock. A 32-worker thread-pool stress run left on_hand == available with no leaked open reservations
Validation happens before any mutation, so a failed call changes nothing. Huge quantities (10**30, 10**100) work. bool, float and str qty are rejected
Reservations from other inventories, copies and fakes are rejected. Settlement uses the recorded sku/qty, not the caller's object
Strong tests: barrier-synchronised concurrency tests (oversell, exactly-once settle, reserve/commit throughput) and a 2000-step seeded model-based random test that checks invariants
./check.sh passes with ruff; 33 tests OK
reports.summary: Build F is a correct, thread-safe implementation that meets every spec point. My probes found no correctness or concurrency bugs: boundaries, invalid, huge and non-numeric inputs, double or cross settlement, foreign or copied reservations, ID reuse after GC, and a 32-thread pool stress run. Tests are thorough and meaningful, including a model-based random test. The remaining issues are minor: AttributeError for a non-dict stock argument, strict rejection of int subclasses, somewhat over-engineered id()-keyed bookkeeping with tests for adversarial forging, and minimal README/docstring coverage. ./check.sh passes.

ranking.rationale: Every spec point passes in my probe: unknown SKU, catalog SKU missing from the dict gives 0, bool/0/float rejected, 10**30 gives OutOfStock, all four double-settle orders raise ReservationError. A 32-thread pool stress run stayed consistent, and 500 reservations settled concurrently twice each gave exactly 500 successes. At 74 lines it is the smallest and most idiomatic: a frozen eq=False dataclass, an identity-keyed _open dict that records sku/qty so a tampered object cannot skew counts, and one lock. The tests are proportionate (23 cases, barrier races) and the README is updated. No blockers or majors.

judge.verdict: All six builds meet the spec and pass ./check.sh. My probes found no correctness or concurrency bugs in any of them, and no inspector claimed a blocker or major defect. D and F come out ahead because they are compact, single-lock designs that settle each reservation by identity using sku/qty recorded inside the inventory. A is equally correct but trusts fields on the reservation object at settle time. C and E are correct but carry more test bloat or quirkier Reservation designs. B ranks last because it sums all open holds under the global lock on every available/reserve call. That cost is quadratic, a real drawback for checkout running in a thread pool.

judges.verdict: All six builds meet the spec. Each passes ./check.sh, my shared spec probe, 10 invariant stress trials with a 1e-6 switch interval, a 1000-thread oversell test and a concurrent settle-once race, and no inspector-claimed blocker or major exists. What separates them is design hygiene. D, A and F are compact, identity-based and clean. B pays O(open holds) under the global lock and carries heavy over-engineering. E's value-equal Reservation lets two distinct holds collapse in a set, although E is the only build whose concurrency tests actually fail when the locks are removed. Every other build's barrier race tests still pass with no locking at all.
